title: Min Stack
interviewTips: Clarify constraints: will pop/top/getMin ever be called on empty stack? Per LeetCode no, but ask about behavior and duplicate values.
Trade-off to discuss: scanning for min is O(n) time vs caching min per state is O(1) time with O(n) extra space; duplicates require <= not < when pushing to min stack.
Edge-case tip: test duplicate minimums e.g., push 0, push 0, pop once — getMin must still be 0, and test strictly decreasing pushes where every element is a new min.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force with Scan for Min
approaches.intuition: Use a normal array/vector as stack for push/pop/top, and compute minimum on demand by scanning all elements when getMin is called. Simplest correct design with no extra bookkeeping.
approaches.theory: A stack natively supports LIFO push/pop/top in O(1). The minimum over the stack is a global aggregate that changes on push/pop. Without caching, the only way to know it is to iterate over all n elements and take the minimum. This is correct because min(stack) is definitionally the answer, but getMin becomes linear.

timeComplexity.complexity: O(n) for getMin, O(1) for push/pop/top
timeComplexity.explanation: push, pop, top touch only the top element. getMin scans all n elements to find the minimum.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only one array storing n pushed values, no auxiliary structure.

dryRunExample.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()

edgeCases: Single element: getMin must return that element
Duplicate minimums: e.g., [0,0] getMin is 0, still correct via scan
Negative and large values (-2^31 to 2^31-1): min comparison must handle full int range

approaches.name: Approach 2: Auxiliary Min Stack
approaches.intuition: Cache the minimum at every stack state in a second stack. When you push a new value that is <= current minimum, also push it onto minStack. When you pop that value, pop minStack too. Then getMin is just the top of minStack.
approaches.theory: Let S be main stack and M be min stack where M.top() = min(S). Invariant: M is non-decreasing from bottom to top and contains exactly the decreasing minima of S. Push maintains it: if val <= M.top(), val becomes new minimum so push to M. Pop maintains it: if popped val == M.top(), that minimum no longer exists so pop M. By induction M.top() always equals min(S), giving O(1) getMin. Using <= (not <) correctly handles duplicate minima.

timeComplexity.explanation: push does at most two pushes, pop does at most two pops, top and getMin are single peek operations.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Main stack holds n elements, min stack holds at most n elements (exactly the number of times a new minimum or equal minimum was pushed; O(n) worst case for decreasing inputs, O(1) for increasing inputs).

dryRunExample.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()
steps: pop: top -3 == min top -3 so pop both -> stack=[-2,0], minStack=[-2]

edgeCases: Duplicate mins: push(0), push(0) must push to minStack twice due to <=, else first pop loses min
Strictly decreasing: e.g., 5,4,3,2,1 — minStack grows to size n, still O(1) per op
Strictly increasing: e.g., 1,2,3 — minStack stays size 1, pop must not touch minStack until 1 is popped
Interleaved push/pop/top: invariant holds after every operation
